what_its_for: Acyclovir is an antiviral medicine used to treat infections caused by the herpes virus. This includes cold sores (oral herpes), genital herpes, chickenpox, and shingles. It helps reduce the severity and length of outbreaks, speeds up healing of sores, and can help prevent future outbreaks if taken regularly. It does not cure herpes, but it does help control it.
how_to_take: Take acyclovir exactly as your doctor tells you. You can take it with or without food, but taking it with food may help if it upsets your stomach. Drink plenty of water while taking this medicine to help protect your kidneys. Swallow tablets or capsules whole. If you are using the liquid form, shake the bottle well and use the measuring spoon or cup that comes with it — do not use a regular kitchen spoon. If you are using the buccal tablet (Sitavig), place it on your gum above a canine tooth (upper front side tooth), hold it in place for 30 seconds, and let it dissolve slowly — do not swallow, chew, or crush it.
dosing: Your dose depends on what condition is being treated, your age, and how well your kidneys work. Common doses are: Cold sores: 400 mg 3 times a day, OR 200 mg 5 times a day, for 5 to 10 days. Genital herpes (first outbreak): 200 mg every 4 hours, 5 times a day for 10 days. Genital herpes (repeat outbreaks): 400 mg 3 times a day for 5 days. Prevention of outbreaks: 400 mg twice daily, long-term. Chickenpox or shingles: higher doses, as directed by your doctor. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions. Take doses evenly spaced throughout the day.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store tablets and capsules at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C to 25°C). Keep them away from heat, direct light, and moisture — do not store in the bathroom. Store the liquid in the refrigerator or at room temperature, depending on the brand — check the label. Keep all medicine out of the reach of children. Do not use medicine that is expired — check the expiration date on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid sexual contact when you have visible sores or active outbreaks, as acyclovir does not fully prevent spreading herpes to others. Always use a condom, even when you have no symptoms, to reduce the risk of transmission. Avoid touching sores and then touching your eyes — wash your hands frequently. Avoid getting dehydrated — drink enough water each day. Let your doctor know if you take other medicines, especially those that can affect your kidneys, such as NSAIDs (like ibuprofen or naproxen) or other antiviral medicines.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you experience: confusion, agitation, or trouble speaking; feeling unusually tired or weak; decreased urination or swelling; hallucinations or seizures; severe skin rash or allergic reaction (hives, swelling of face or throat, difficulty breathing); unusual bruising or bleeding; or if your symptoms are not improving or are getting worse. These could be signs of serious side effects that need immediate attention.
when_it_works: Acyclovir works best when started as soon as possible after symptoms begin — ideally within 48 to 72 hours of the first sign of an outbreak such as tingling, itching, or burning. It does not work instantly. You may start to feel better within 2 to 3 days, but sores may take 7 to 10 days to fully heal. If you take it for prevention, it works continuously to reduce how often outbreaks happen.
special_populations: Older adults and people with kidney problems may need a lower dose, since the kidneys process this medicine. Your doctor may do blood tests to check your kidney function. Pregnant women should talk to their doctor before taking acyclovir — it is sometimes used during pregnancy if the benefits outweigh the risks, especially near the time of delivery to prevent passing herpes to the baby. Acyclovir can pass into breast milk, so breastfeeding mothers should discuss risks and benefits with their doctor. Children can take acyclovir for chickenpox or herpes, but the dose is based on their weight, so always follow the doctor's instructions carefully.
